text:
The take that many NVIDIA supply deals were "a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract" is half right.

Jensen did made the big calls in the room. CEOs of some of NVIDIA's largest customers told me that this past week. Billion-dollar commitments, made on the spot. I'd bet suppliers saw the same. That is hard to replace.

What's overstated is the risk to the biggest deals. They're on paper.

• NVIDIA disclosed $279B in supply and capacity commitments as of July, up from $119B a quarter earlier, driven by memory. $267B of it is scheduled through fiscal 2029. You can’t report it without more than a handshake. 
• NVIDIA became TSMC's largest customer in 2025. The two biggest HBM suppliers are tightening contracts so buyers can't back out. Suppliers aren't the flight risk.
• I've said supply and the roadmap are mostly set for at least 18 months.

The real exposure is the next round: anything not on paper, and whether NVIDIA keeps committing at Jensen's pace. Rivals will bid for whatever it doesn't.

NVIDIA has a deep bench, and Colette Kress has been on calls reassuring suppliers. Tuesday's $NVDA call, her first as interim CEO, is where she shows who makes the big calls now.

La bible de l'investissement value, le livre qui a formé Buffett. Monsieur Marché, la marge de sécurité, la différence entre investir et spéculer -- Assez dense mais les commentaires de Zweig aident -- Débutant motivé à intermédiaire

C'est l'histoire romancée de Jesse Livermore, le plus grand spéculateur de son époque -- Très facilement lisible -- Plutôt pour quelqu'un qui débute

Comment repérer les grandes boîtes de croissance et les garder des années, avec sa fameuse méthode des 15 points -- Court et clair -- Débutant à intermédiaire

Les meilleures lettres de Buffett aux actionnaires, classées par thème -- Simple à lire, à picorer -- Tous niveaux

Pourquoi il est si dur de battre le marché, et l'argument pour les ETF indiciels -- Très accessible -- Débutant

La mécanique des bulles et des krachs financiers sur quatre siècles -- Assez académique -- Intermédiaire à avancé

en_summary: The intuition Dwarkesh was pointing to is that AI research progress is produced by a combination of researcher effort and exp...」
text:
Ok I thought about this a bit more. It took me a while to finally understand what @dwarkesh_sp was getting at by casting the discussion into a formal economics model. We were simply talking past each other.

Fundamentally, the “intuition” Dwarkesh was pointing to is that AI research progress is produced by a combination of researcher effort and experiment compute that are imperfect substitutes. The production function of AI capability is concave (“isoquants” are convex), so using a more balanced mix is always more productive for a given budget than being stuck in a corner.

Research automation changes this in two distinct ways. First, it raises the effective quantity of the researcher input since automated researchers work much faster and continuously, so each one delivers say “50×” more researcher input per calendar week. Because of concavity, that does not translate into a 50× speedup in final research output for a fixed compute budget; Dwarkesh’s rough lower bound is still something like “5×”.

Second, and perhaps more importantly, automation also raises the productivity of the AI capability production process itself. It’s almost like there’s a technology or productivity multiplier that rises with each generation of smarter models. Once models match the best humans, every automated researcher is at the level of today’s top researchers (in his words), and the work is modular enough to be highly parallelized. (I’m not sure whether this last part is really even necessary.)

T

zh_summary: If AI is really so critical that being just a few years behind is a matter of life and death, then China could blow the whole thing up right now. For example, China could restrict rare-earth exports, take over Taiwan to prevent the U.S. from getting advanced chips, and disrupt the supply of many other critical components. My point is, I don’t think China sees AI that way. I think they’re willing to fall a few years behind while their domestic chip manufacturing catches up. Importing downgraded NVIDIA chips wouldn’t do much to help them achieve their long-term goals. And I don’t think China is thinking small, either. They probably want to dominate the global AI market in the future, not just their domestic market. That’s why I think they’re playing the long game.
